thread.title: The Market Doesn't Care About Facebook - Facebook (NASDAQ:FB)

author: Michael Wiggins De Oliveira
title: The Market Doesn't Care About Facebook - Facebook (NASDAQ:FB)
text:
Investment Thesis Facebook ( FB ) is highly free cash flow generative, with each quarter's cash dropping to its balance sheet. Furthermore, and possibly important, Facebook's stock is cheap right now, but it will not remain cheap for long.
Recent Developments With constant bombarding of negative news during Facebook's Cambridge Analytica scandal, and the market sold off from Facebook causing its share price lose vitality. At the time, the stock easily lost over 20% from its January-February highs.
However, impressively, the stock has regained all that ground in a very short period of time - which reinforces my view, that there is still a lot of investor appetite for Facebook, and so there should be.
For example, roughly a year ago, Facebook's market cap stood at $420 billion while Facebook carried a net cash position of approximately $32 billion. Fast forward to today, and granted that its market cap is slightly higher at $555 billion, but its balance sheet as of quarter end carried a net cash position of roughly $44 billion. Said another way, whereas Facebook's share price has risen by roughly 25%, its cash is now up more than 35% - implying that investors have not 'missed the boat' on Facebook and that the market's present valuation is not fully reflecting Facebook's full potential.
Facebook's Future Prospects CEO Zuckerberg spent a large chunk of Facebook's Q1 2018 earnings call highlighting to investors the strong potential that AI will bring to Facebook. Zuckerberg described how AI can help Facebook gather context of what is being shared on its platform, but was quick to explain that Facebook's purpose was to ensure it made it easier for users to make connections and conversations with each other.
Obviously, Zuckerberg deemed it necessary at the time of the call (mid Cambridge Analytica fiasco) to highlight positive strides that AI brings, such as the ability to discern context that can help in the fight against terrorism, and how Facebook is able to detect ISIS and Al Qaeda-related terror content and remove 99% of this content before any person flags it up to Facebook.
Moreover, on the Q&A section of the call, Zuckerberg did highlight how Facebook would not look to simply stop at the moderation of content, but how it was looking to hire tens of thousands of staff to work on AI - highlighting just meaningful Zuckerberg thinks AI is likely to be for the future of Facebook. However, at the same time, Facebook does not wish to make too much noise about its advanced capabilities in AI, as it does not wish to gain any more spotlight over its AI capabilities. In fact, Zuckerberg was quick to play down Facebook's abilities in AI and describe that its competitors also had many of the same tools as Facebook.
Valuation
Source: author's calculations, morningstar.com
The above table highlights two very interesting attributes.
Firstly, Facebook's P/S ratio and P/Cash Flow ratios are presently cheaper than their own 5-year average. This is important, particularly when it comes to the P/S ratio. Why? Because I find that the P/Sales ratio cuts through a lot of noise. Essentially, even with a high-growth company such as Facebook, the lower down the income statement we look, the more volatility it has from year to year. However, the reverse is also generally true; Facebook's revenue stream will not be anywhere near as volatile as other lines lower down Facebook's income statement.
Furthermore, if we compare the Facebook of today with the Facebook from 5 years ago, we can see that, for FY 2013, Facebook generated less than $8 billion in revenue accompanied with operating margins of 35.6%. Now, as of FY 2017, Facebook's revenue stood at just over $40 billion, and its operating margins have soared to 49.7%. So, here is the irony. We can see that, for all intents and purposes, Facebook is presently performing financially better than 5 years ago, yet its P/S ratio for its 5-year average was higher in the past than it is at the moment.
Secondly, the above table includes amongst its peer group Nvidia ( NVDA ). I have included Nvidia, which obviously does not compete with Facebook in advertising, but it certainly has a lot of exposure to AI, and all the narrative currently surrounding AI and how Nvidia is going to benefit so much from AI tailwinds. And we can see how investors are more than happy to pay nearly 3 times its 5-year average, currently paying up 15.2X its P/Sales ratio vs. historically paying on average only 5.2X its P/Sales ratio. The same idea presents itself, but to a lesser extent, with Apple ( AAPL ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ) ( GOOG ) (note: as I have argued elsewhere on SA, I think that Apple's and Alphabet's are also undervalued).
Takeaway Facebook offers investors a rare opportunity in its history to profit from AI without having to pay a heavy price tag for its stock.
